HOLD: There is a problem. Default arguments in Python are evaluated exactly once, when the function is defined, not each time it's called. The same list object is reused across calls.

What would change my mind: Running the code and showing me that a second call to `add(1)` returns `[1]` instead of `[1, 1]`. It won't.

This is the opposite direction of the common myth — people often incorrectly think defaults are fresh each time, when they're actually static.

grade.note: Correctly holds that default mutable arguments are evaluated once and cites the observable behavior as evidence.
